group.title: Business and management
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To change the way a company or system is organized, usually to make it work better.
examples: The firm plans to {restructure} its sales teams next year.
wrong: They restructured the company by leaving every team exactly as it was.

words.meaning: The buying of one company by another.
examples: The {acquisition} of the smaller rival made them market leader.
wrong: After the acquisition, the two companies had nothing to do with each other.

words.meaning: A company that is owned and controlled by a larger company.
examples: The bank runs its insurance business through a {subsidiary}.
wrong: The subsidiary owns and controls the parent company that set it up.

words.meaning: How easily a business can get cash to pay what it owes soon.
examples: Selling the warehouse improved the company’s {liquidity}.
wrong: Their liquidity was excellent, so they could not pay a single bill.

words.meaning: Preparing people inside a company to take over key jobs when current leaders leave.
examples: Good {succession planning} meant the new CEO was ready on day one.
wrong: Thanks to succession planning, nobody was ready when the director retired.

words.meaning: The ability of a business or system to grow easily without breaking down.
examples: Investors asked about the {scalability} of the app before they put money in.
wrong: The scalability of the plan means it can never grow beyond ten customers.

words.meaning: To start offering new kinds of products or services so a business depends less on one.
examples: The farm {diversified} into tourism and cheese making.
wrong: They diversified by selling only one product to one customer.

words.meaning: A large company made up of many firms in different kinds of business.
examples: The {conglomerate} owns hotels, banks and a shipping line.
wrong: The conglomerate is a tiny shop that sells only one product.

words.meaning: How possible and practical it is to do something successfully.
examples: We ran a {feasibility} study before building the new plant.
wrong: The feasibility study proved the plan could not be checked at all.

words.meaning: A possible future problem that you plan for in case it happens.
examples: Keep some money aside for {contingencies}.
wrong: A contingency is an event that is certain to happen every day.

words.meaning: The detailed planning and moving of goods, people and supplies.
examples: The {logistics} of shipping fresh food abroad are complicated.
wrong: Logistics is the art of never planning how goods arrive.

words.meaning: A new business activity that involves some risk.
examples: Her first business {venture} was a small coffee cart.
wrong: The venture was completely safe and needed no money at all.

words.meaning: The final profit or loss of a business; also the most important point.
examples: Cutting energy costs improved our {bottom line}.
wrong: The bottom line was a small detail that nobody cared about.

words.meaning: The part of all sales in a market that one company makes.
examples: The new phone helped the company grow its {market share}.
wrong: Their market share was the money they spent on office plants.

words.meaning: Giving good results for the money spent.
examples: Online ads proved more {cost-effective} than television.
wrong: The cost-effective plan wasted huge sums and achieved nothing.

words.meaning: The job of watching and checking that work is done properly.
examples: The project needs stronger {oversight} from senior managers.
wrong: With strict oversight, nobody ever checked the work.

words.meaning: How confident and positive the people in a team or group feel.
examples: Staff {morale} rose after the bonus was announced.
wrong: Morale was high, so everyone felt hopeless and wanted to quit.

words.meaning: A company’s success in keeping its staff or customers.
examples: Flexible hours have improved staff {retention}.
wrong: Good retention means most workers leave within a month.

words.meaning: To lead an important plan, campaign or activity.
examples: She {spearheaded} the move into Asian markets.
wrong: He spearheaded the project by following quietly at the back.

words.meaning: The money and benefits someone is paid for their work.
examples: The board approved the director’s {remuneration} package.
wrong: Her remuneration was the unpaid work she did for free.

words.meaning: To control every small detail of other people’s work too closely.
examples: Good leaders trust their staff and don’t {micromanage} them.
wrong: My boss micromanages, so she never checks what we do.

words.meaning: To give someone the confidence or authority to make decisions.
examples: The new policy {empowers} teams to set their own goals.
wrong: The rules empowered staff by taking away all their choices.

words.meaning: To work with and keep in contact with another person or group.
examples: Our office will {liaise} with the suppliers about delivery dates.
wrong: She liaised with the client by refusing to speak to them.

words.meaning: To use a situation to gain an advantage (often ’on’ something).
examples: The shop {capitalized} on the warm weather by selling fans.
wrong: They capitalized on the trend by ignoring it completely.

words.meaning: The act of ending workers’ jobs because there is not enough work or money.
examples: The {layoffs} affected almost a third of the staff.
wrong: The layoff gave every worker a new job and a pay rise.

words.meaning: To make careful plans to reach a goal.
examples: The managers met to {strategize} for the coming year.
wrong: We strategized by acting at random without any plan.

words.meaning: A short written description of a company’s aims and values.
examples: Our {mission statement} promises honest prices for everyone.
wrong: The mission statement listed the company’s parking spaces.

words.meaning: A piece of work or product that must be finished and handed over in a project.
examples: The first {deliverable} is a full report due in March.
wrong: A deliverable is a task that nobody ever needs to finish.

words.meaning: Lower costs for each item that a business gets by producing a lot.
examples: Big supermarkets enjoy {economies of scale} that small shops cannot match.
wrong: Thanks to economies of scale, each item cost more as they made more.

words.meaning: The total number of people who work for an organization.
examples: The firm cut its {headcount} by ten percent.
wrong: Our headcount is the number of meetings we hold each week.

words.meaning: The order of authority in an organization, from top to bottom.
examples: Complaints should go up the {chain of command}.
wrong: In a chain of command, everyone has exactly the same authority.

words.meaning: A business project that two or more companies run together and share.
examples: The two carmakers set up a {joint venture} to build batteries.
wrong: The joint venture was run by one company with no partners.

words.meaning: Careful checking of facts and risks before a deal or decision.
examples: Buyers must do {due diligence} before signing the contract.
wrong: They did due diligence by signing the deal without reading it.

words.meaning: A company’s plan for how it will make money.
examples: Their {business model} depends on monthly subscriptions.
wrong: The business model explained how the firm would lose money forever.

words.meaning: Something a company does especially well that gives it an advantage.
examples: Customer service is our {core competency}.
wrong: Our core competency is the thing we do worst of all.

words.meaning: A personal reason, often financial, for wanting something to happen.
examples: The landlord has a {vested interest} in keeping rents high.
wrong: He had a vested interest in the result, so he didn’t care how it ended.

words.meaning: The share of the selling price that is left as profit after costs.
examples: Luxury goods often have a high {profit margin}.
wrong: The profit margin is the part of the price spent on costs.

words.meaning: The profit you get compared with the money you put in.
examples: The new machines gave a quick {return on investment}.
wrong: The return on investment was the money they spent at the start.

words.meaning: To do less well than expected or than others.
examples: The store {underperformed} and missed its sales target.
wrong: The team underperformed by beating every target they had.

words.meaning: Happening or produced every three months.
examples: The {quarterly} report shows strong growth.
wrong: The quarterly meeting is held once every ten years.
